learn.hook: Your football may be designed in one country, stitched in another and sold in a third — all by one company!
points: Until about the middle of the 20th century, production was organised mostly within countries. What crossed borders were raw materials, food and finished goods. Colonies like India exported raw materials and food and imported finished goods.

A Multinational Corporation (MNC) is a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation. MNCs set up offices and factories where they can get cheaper labour and other resources, to lower costs and earn more profit.
MNCs choose places that are close to markets, have skilled and unskilled labour at low cost, have other factors of production available, and have government policies that look after their interests.
Investment is money spent to buy assets such as land, buildings, machines and equipment. Investment made by MNCs is called foreign investment.

MNCs spread production by: setting up production jointly with local companies (bringing money for new machines and the latest technology); buying up local companies, which is the most common route; and placing orders with small producers, for example for garments, footwear and sports goods, which the MNC then sells under its own brand name.
Foreign trade connects markets: producers can sell beyond their own country, and buyers get more choice. For example, toys made in China are sold in Indian markets.

example.q: Think it through: A foreign company that makes mobile phones wants to open a factory in Asia. Why might it choose a city in India?
steps: India has a very large market of buyers close by.
It has many skilled engineers and workers at relatively low wages.
If roads, ports, power and government policies are favourable, costs fall further.
Lower costs and a big market mean higher profits for the MNC.
example.answer: Because of a large nearby market, low-cost skilled labour and supportive facilities and policies.

learn.reallife: Look at the label on your school bag, shoes or toy: 'Made in India' for a foreign brand, or 'Made in China' on a toy sold in your local market, shows production spread across countries.

quiz.q: What is a Multinational Corporation (MNC)?
options: A company that sells only in its home country
A company owned by many people in one town
A company that owns or controls production in more than one nation
A government department that collects taxes
quiz.explain: An MNC's production is spread across more than one country.
steps: Asked: the meaning of an MNC.
An MNC owns or controls production in more than one nation.
'Multinational' means many nations, not many owners.
Answer: A company that owns or controls production in more than one nation
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'multinational' refers to many owners rather than many nations

quiz.q: Why do MNCs set up production in countries like India?
options: To get cheaper skilled labour and be close to large markets
Because they are forced to by the United Nations
Because there are no markets in their own countries
quiz.explain: Low-cost skilled labour and nearness to big markets reduce costs and increase profits.
steps: Asked: why MNCs set up production in countries like India.
MNCs go where labour and resources are cheaper and markets are near, to cut costs.
Lower costs mean more profit.
So cheaper skilled labour and nearness to large markets is the reason.
quiz.mistake: Does not link MNC decisions to lower costs and profits

quiz.q: According to the textbook, what is the most common route for MNC investment?
options: Placing orders only with large government firms
Buying up local companies and then expanding production
quiz.explain: MNCs most often buy existing local companies, which gives them ready factories and markets.
steps: Asked: the most common route of MNC investment.
MNCs spread production by joint production, buying local companies, or placing orders.
The textbook says buying up local companies is the most common route.
Free loans or schools are not ways of spreading production.
Answer: Buying up local companies and then expanding production
quiz.mistake: Picks a different way of spreading production as the most common

quiz.q: What is 'foreign investment'?
options: Money Indians spend on foreign holidays
quiz.explain: Investment means buying assets like land, buildings and machines; when MNCs do it, it is foreign investment.
steps: Asked: the meaning of foreign investment.
Investment is money spent to buy assets like land, buildings and machines.
Investment made by MNCs is called foreign investment.
Holiday spending or loans from relatives are not investment by MNCs.
Answer: Investment made by MNCs
quiz.mistake: Thinks any spending abroad is foreign investment

quiz.q: A large foreign brand places orders with small garment makers in Tiruppur and sells the shirts under its own name. Which way of spreading production is this?
options: Placing orders for production with small producers
quiz.explain: The MNC does not own these units; it gets goods made by small producers and sells them under its brand.
steps: Given: the brand gets small Tiruppur units to make shirts and sells them under its own name.
The MNC does not own or buy these units.
This is placing orders for production with small producers.
quiz.mistake: Confuses placing orders with owning or buying companies

quiz.q: How can joint production with an MNC benefit a local Indian company?
options: It makes the local company pay no wages
It stops the local company from producing
The MNC can provide money for new machines and the latest technology
It closes the local company's market
quiz.explain: In joint production, the MNC brings additional investment, such as faster machines, and the latest technology.
steps: Asked: how joint production helps a local company.
In joint production the MNC brings money for new machines.
It also brings the latest technology, which helps the local firm produce more and better.
Answer: The MNC can provide money for new machines and the latest technology
quiz.mistake: Assumes partnership with an MNC only harms local firms

quiz.q: Before the middle of the 20th century, what did colonies like India mainly export?
quiz.explain: Colonies exported raw materials and food and imported finished goods.
steps: Asked: what colonies like India exported before the mid-20th century.
Production was mostly within countries; raw materials, food and finished goods crossed borders.
Colonies exported raw materials and food and imported finished goods.
Software or cars are modern exports, not colonial ones.
Answer: Raw materials and food
quiz.mistake: Applies present-day exports to the colonial period

quiz.q: How does foreign trade help buyers?
options: It reduces the choice of goods
It makes all goods more expensive
It stops goods from other countries entering
It gives them a wider choice of goods beyond what is made at home
quiz.explain: Foreign trade brings goods from other countries, so buyers have more choice.
steps: Asked: how foreign trade helps buyers.
Foreign trade brings in goods made in other countries, like toys from China.
So buyers get a wider choice than goods made only at home.
Answer: It gives them a wider choice of goods beyond what is made at home
quiz.mistake: Thinks trade only benefits producers

teach.ask: Gappu found a toy with a foreign brand but 'Made in India' on it: 'How can that be? What is an MNC?'
teach.praise: Tweet! An MNC controls production in more than one country to cut costs and earn profits — by joint production, buying local firms or placing orders. Superb!
teach.nudge: In how many countries does an MNC produce? And why does it choose a particular country?

revise.summary: An MNC owns or controls production in more than one nation. It sets up where labour is cheap and markets are near, to cut costs and raise profits, through joint production, buying local companies or placing orders. Foreign trade gives buyers more choice.

remember: MNC: owns or controls production in more than one nation
Investment made by MNCs is called foreign investment
Ways: joint production with local companies, buying up local companies (most common), placing orders with small producers
Colonies like India exported raw materials and food and imported finished goods
traps: 'Multinational' means many nations, not many owners

learn.hook: A call centre worker in Bengaluru can help a customer on another continent at midnight — welcome to a connected world!
points: Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries, mainly through more foreign trade and more foreign investment by MNCs. Goods, services, investments and technology move across countries; the movement of people is still limited.

Technology made it possible: faster and cheaper transport (containers carry goods on ships, trains, planes and trucks), and information and communication technology — telecommunications, computers and the internet. A magazine can be designed in Delhi and printed in Mumbai; call centres serve customers abroad.

A trade barrier is a restriction on trade set by the government, such as a tax on imports or a limit on how much can be imported. It lets the government decide which goods and how much of them enter the country.
After independence, India put barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment to protect its young industries from foreign competition.

Around 1991, India made big changes in its economic policy and removed barriers on trade and investment to a large extent. Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is called liberalisation. Indian producers now had to compete with foreign producers, which was expected to push them to improve quality.

example.q: Think it through: The government puts a heavy tax on imported toys. What happens to toy prices and to Indian toy makers?
steps: The import tax makes foreign toys costlier in Indian shops.
Fewer people buy imported toys.
Indian toy makers face less competition and sell more.
This is how a trade barrier protects domestic producers — and removing it (liberalisation) brings more competition.
example.answer: Imported toys become costlier, so Indian makers are protected; the tax is a trade barrier.

learn.reallife: Video calls with relatives working in the Gulf, or an online order shipped from another country, show how technology links people and markets across the world.

quiz.q: What is globalisation?
options: Rapid integration or interconnection between countries through trade and investment
Making goods only for the local market
Closing a country's borders to trade
quiz.explain: Globalisation links countries closely through more foreign trade and foreign investment by MNCs.
steps: Asked: the meaning of globalisation.
Globalisation is rapid integration or interconnection between countries.
It happens mainly through more foreign trade and foreign investment by MNCs.
Closing borders or local-only trade is the opposite.
Answer: Rapid integration or interconnection between countries through trade and investment
quiz.mistake: Confuses globalisation with protection or local trade

quiz.q: Under globalisation, the movement of which of these between countries is still limited?
quiz.explain: Goods, services, investment and technology move fairly freely, but countries still restrict the movement of people.
steps: Asked: what still moves in a limited way between countries.
Goods, services, investment and technology move across countries fairly freely.
The movement of people is still limited, because countries restrict it.
quiz.mistake: Assumes everything moves equally freely

quiz.q: Which development in technology has helped globalisation the most in services like call centres?
options: Information and communication technology, such as the internet
quiz.explain: Telecommunications, computers and the internet let services be provided instantly across countries.
steps: Asked: the technology behind services like call centres.
Telecommunications, computers and the internet are information and communication technology.
They let services be given instantly to customers abroad.
Bullock carts, letters by sea and ledgers are too slow.
Answer: Information and communication technology, such as the internet
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the internet with global services

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of a trade barrier?
options: A bank loan to a farmer
quiz.explain: A tax on imports restricts trade by making foreign goods costlier.
steps: Asked: an example of a trade barrier.
A trade barrier is a government restriction on trade, such as a tax on imports or a limit on imports.
A tax on imported goods is such a restriction.
A highway, an online shop or a farm loan is not a restriction on trade.
Answer: A tax on imported goods
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything related to trade is a barrier

quiz.q: Why did India put barriers on foreign trade and investment after independence?
options: To protect domestic producers from foreign competition
Because there were no goods in the world
quiz.explain: Indian industries were just starting, so the government shielded them from strong foreign competition.
steps: Asked: why India had trade barriers after independence.
Indian industries were young and just starting.
Barriers protected these domestic producers from foreign competition.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the aim of the barriers

quiz.q: Around which year did India remove barriers on foreign trade and investment to a large extent?
quiz.explain: Major changes in economic policy were made around 1991.
steps: Asked: the year of major liberalisation in India.
India made big changes in economic policy around 1991.
It removed barriers on trade and investment to a large extent then.
1947 is independence, not liberalisation.
Answer: 1991
quiz.mistake: Confuses 1991 with independence or other years

quiz.q: What does 'liberalisation' mean?
options: Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government
quiz.explain: Liberalisation means freeing trade and investment from government restrictions.
steps: Asked: the meaning of liberalisation.
Liberalisation is removing barriers or restrictions set by the government.
Adding barriers or taking over companies is the opposite.
Answer: Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government
quiz.mistake: Confuses liberalisation with protection or nationalisation

quiz.q: What did liberalisation mean for Indian producers?
options: They no longer had any competition
They had to compete with foreign producers, which pushed them to improve quality
They had to close all their factories
quiz.explain: With barriers removed, foreign goods entered India, so Indian producers faced competition and had to improve.
steps: Asked: the effect of liberalisation on Indian producers.
With barriers removed, foreign goods entered India.
So Indian producers had to compete with foreign producers.
This competition was expected to push them to improve quality.
Answer: They had to compete with foreign producers, which pushed them to improve quality
quiz.mistake: Thinks removing barriers reduces competition

teach.ask: Gappu read the word 'liberalisation' in a newspaper: 'Is it about birds being set free? What happened in 1991?'
teach.praise: Chirrup! Liberalisation means removing government barriers on trade and investment — India did this around 1991, and technology sped up globalisation. Excellent!

revise.summary: Globalisation is rapid integration of countries through foreign trade and foreign investment, helped by faster transport and information technology. India had trade barriers after independence, but around 1991 it liberalised by removing many of them.

topics.title: WTO, impact of globalisation and fair globalisation

learn.hook: Globalisation is like a big cricket tournament — great if the rules are fair for every team, not just the strongest!
points: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) aims to liberalise international trade. Started at the initiative of developed countries, it sets rules for international trade and checks that they are obeyed.

Critics say WTO rules have been unfair: developed countries have kept their own trade barriers while pushing developing countries to remove theirs. The textbook's example: the US government gives large sums of money to its farmers, so they can sell farm products abroad at very low prices, which hurts farmers in developing countries.

Who gained in India: well-off consumers (more choice, better quality, lower prices); MNCs increased investment in mobile phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food and banking in cities; local companies supplying MNCs; some large Indian companies became MNCs themselves; IT service companies got new opportunities.

Who faced difficulties: many small producers — for example of batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products and vegetable oil — faced tough competition and some shut down. Many workers now get only temporary, flexible jobs with long hours and little security.

To attract foreign companies, the government set up Special Economic Zones (SEZs) with world-class facilities — electricity, water, roads, transport, storage, recreation and education. According to the textbook, companies setting up units in SEZs do not pay taxes for an initial period of five years.

Fair globalisation creates opportunities for all and shares the benefits better. The government can make sure labour laws are followed, support small producers, use trade and investment barriers if needed, and join other developing countries to bargain for fairer WTO rules. People's organisations and campaigns can also make a difference.

example.q: Think it through: Cheap imported toys flood the market. Small toy makers in a town are losing business. What could make globalisation fairer for them?
steps: Consumers gain from cheaper toys, but the small producers lose income.
The government could help small makers improve quality and lower costs with cheap credit and better technology.
If needed, it could use a trade barrier, such as an import tax, to give them time to become competitive.
It could also negotiate at the WTO for fairer rules for developing countries.
example.answer: Support small producers, use barriers where needed, and bargain for fair rules — so benefits are shared by all.

learn.reallife: Wooden toys from Channapatna in Karnataka and Etikoppaka in Andhra Pradesh compete with imported toys; support for such small producers is part of making globalisation fair.

games.title: WTO and fair globalisation: true or false?
items: The WTO aims to liberalise international trade.
Its rules are meant to reduce barriers to trade between countries.
The WTO was started at the initiative of developing countries.
It was started at the initiative of developed countries.
Some developed countries have kept trade barriers while asking developing countries to remove theirs.
This is a key reason why WTO rules are called unfair.
Every person in India gained equally from globalisation.
Well-off consumers and big companies gained more; many small producers and workers faced difficulties.
According to the textbook, companies setting up units in SEZs do not pay taxes for an initial period of five years.
The textbook describes this tax benefit as a way to attract companies to SEZs.
Fair globalisation means benefits are shared by all, not just a few.
It aims to create opportunities for everyone.

quiz.q: What is the main aim of the World Trade Organisation (WTO)?
options: To issue currency for all countries
To build roads in developing countries
quiz.explain: The WTO sets rules to reduce barriers in international trade and makes sure they are followed.
steps: Asked: the main aim of the WTO.
The WTO aims to liberalise international trade.
It sets rules for trade and checks that they are obeyed.
It does not issue currency or give farm loans.
Answer: To liberalise international trade
quiz.mistake: Confuses the WTO with banks or development agencies

quiz.q: At whose initiative was the WTO started?
quiz.explain: The WTO was set up at the initiative of developed countries.
steps: Asked: at whose initiative the WTO was started.
The WTO was started at the initiative of developed countries.
quiz.mistake: Assumes it was started by developing countries

quiz.q: Why are WTO rules often said to be unfair to developing countries?
options: Developed countries have kept their own trade barriers while pushing developing countries to remove theirs
Developing countries are not allowed to export anything
The WTO gives all its money to poor countries
quiz.explain: Developed countries, for example through large farm subsidies, protect their producers while developing countries are asked to open up.
steps: Asked: why WTO rules are called unfair.
Developed countries have kept their own trade barriers.
At the same time they push developing countries to remove theirs.
This double standard is the unfairness.
Answer: Developed countries have kept their own trade barriers while pushing developing countries to remove theirs
quiz.mistake: Misses the double standard in trade rules

quiz.q: The textbook mentions that the US government gives large sums to its farmers. What is the effect on farmers in developing countries?
options: They get higher prices for their crops
They receive the same money from the US
They lose out, because cheap US farm products lower the prices they can get
quiz.explain: Subsidised US farmers can sell at very low prices, so farmers in developing countries struggle to compete.
steps: Asked: the effect of US farm subsidies on farmers in developing countries.
US farmers get large sums from their government, so they can sell farm products abroad very cheaply.
This lowers the prices farmers in developing countries can get.
So those farmers lose out.
Answer: They lose out, because cheap US farm products lower the prices they can get
quiz.mistake: Does not see how subsidies abroad affect prices for other farmers

quiz.q: Which group of consumers has benefited most from globalisation in India?
quiz.explain: Well-off urban consumers enjoy more choice, better quality and lower prices.
steps: Asked: which consumers gained most from globalisation.
Well-off consumers, especially in cities, got more choice, better quality and lower prices.
Small toy and vegetable oil makers and temporary workers faced difficulties.
Answer: Well-off consumers, especially in cities
quiz.mistake: Mixes up consumers who gained with producers who lost

quiz.q: According to the textbook, for how long are companies that set up units in SEZs exempt from taxes?
quiz.explain: Companies in Special Economic Zones do not pay taxes for an initial period of five years.
steps: Asked: the tax-free period for SEZ units, as the textbook says.
The textbook says companies in SEZs pay no taxes for an initial period of five years.
So the answer is 5 years.
quiz.mistake: Guesses the period instead of recalling the five-year tax holiday

quiz.q: What does 'fair globalisation' mean?
options: Only developed countries should set the rules
It should create opportunities for all and share the benefits better
quiz.explain: Fair globalisation aims for everyone, including small producers and workers, to benefit.
steps: Asked: the meaning of fair globalisation.
Fair globalisation creates opportunities for all.
It shares the benefits better, including with small producers and workers.
Helping only big firms or stopping trade is not fair globalisation.
Answer: It should create opportunities for all and share the benefits better
quiz.mistake: Thinks fairness means stopping trade or helping only the powerful

quiz.q: Which government step would help make globalisation fairer?
options: Ignoring labour laws so companies can save money
Removing all support for small producers
Ensuring labour laws are properly implemented so workers get their rights
Letting developed countries alone decide trade rules
quiz.explain: Proper labour laws protect workers, which helps share the benefits of globalisation more fairly.
steps: Asked: a step that makes globalisation fairer.
The government can make sure labour laws are properly followed.
This gives workers their rights and shares the benefits more fairly.
Ignoring laws or removing support for small producers increases unfairness.
Answer: Ensuring labour laws are properly implemented so workers get their rights
quiz.mistake: Chooses a step that would increase unfairness

teach.ask: Gappu is worried: 'My cousin's small toy shop is losing to cheap imported toys. Is globalisation good or bad? What can make it fair?'
teach.praise: Hurray! Globalisation helped some and hurt others; fair rules at the WTO, labour laws and support for small producers can share the benefits with all. Brilliant!

In India, well-off consumers and many companies gained, while small producers and workers faced difficulties. Fair globalisation shares benefits with all.
